  - entries match bare id *and* `kind/id`; a missing file, broken JSON, or an identity with no entry
    means **nothing readable** (fail closed);
  - the filter sits inside the retrieval **predicate** and in the by-id fetch, and a refusal must be
    indistinguishable from absence (same exception, same audit action) or the ids can be enumerated;
  - **references are scrubbed too** — a visible record's `source`/`provenance` can name a withheld
    record by id, and this deployment's ids carry the operator's name
    (`experience:exp-wsl-<owner>-…`), so the by-id path leaked the withheld subject while the record
    list looked clean. Found only by a second scan of the *visible* set for identifying strings and
    for references pointing at withheld ids — scan the negative space, not just the withheld set.
  - choosing the list: keyword-scan the approved corpus for the operator's name, handles and business
    identifiers, then read every hit in full before deciding — a boundary looks different in context.
    A first pass over the 22 approved records withheld 12 and left 10; records that merely describe
    the platform's internals were left readable and flagged to the operator as a second decision.
  - verify on the real corpus, not in tests alone: enumerate the store's record list and evaluate the
    check per record (a count taken from a search result only covers what the query matched), in both
    directions — external identity loses the listed records, owner's view unchanged.
- **Quota** (command allowlist × count × time window) — Hermes ships no quota mechanism; implement it as
  a `hooks.pre_tool_call` **shell hook** with `fail_closed: true`. Shape that works: the script reads the
  JSON payload on stdin and answers `{"action":"block","message":...}` or `{}`; it keeps counts in a
  state file under its own `HERMES_HOME` and appends one audit line per call. Traps: that file is
  read-modify-write from a short-lived process that runs **concurrently** inside one conversation — lock
  it (`O_CREAT|O_EXCL` + stale-lock reclaim) or the count silently under-reports; an unreadable/broken
  state file must count as failure, never as "zero used today"; and three independent ceilings (per day,
  per session, per rolling minute) catch different failure modes — a burst cap that fires on calls a few
  seconds apart breaks normal consecutive tool calls, so size it far above normal cadence. Non-TTY runs
  (gateway, cron) never see the consent prompt: pre-seed `<HERMES_HOME>/shell-hooks-allowlist.json` as an
  `approvals` array of `{event, command}`, the command string **byte-identical** to the config entry, or
  the hook silently stays unregistered. Deploy the hooks directory into the guest's own `HERMES_HOME`,
  have the installer rewrite path prefixes when copying config, then assert no operator-home path
  survives the copy. Also narrow the tool surface itself: a borrowed runtime should not hold tools that
  leave persistent state or drive the operator's desktop — deny them in the hook as well, so a later
  config edit cannot silently re-grant them.
- **The entry path** (tunnel / reverse proxy) — independent of identity, and the operator decides it.
  Keep the bind loopback: Tailscale's `serve` documents that only `http://127.0.0.1` is a valid proxy
  target, so the tunnel and the "never widen the bind" rule agree. Declaring a non-loopback
  `public_url` **engages the auth gate and fails closed at startup without a password provider** — write
  the credentials *before* the public URL, or the symptom handed to the guest is "the service will not
  start" and gets blamed on the tunnel. This is also why the local SPA session token is deliberately
  useless as a remote credential.

  Reaching a *person* (rather than a tunnel you control yourself) is a different mechanism: share the
  host machine into their tailnet. The facts that decide the plan, all worth stating **before** the
  operator clicks: the share link is `https://login.tailscale.com/admin/invite/<code>`, **30 days and
  single-use by default**, and it is a credential ("treat it the way you would a password") — send it
  out of band, never as chat text. The recipient must be an **owner/admin of her own tailnet** (no
  matching account needed) and reaches the host **only by FQDN** `<host>.<your-tailnet>.ts.net`, with
  MagicDNS on. The direction is one-way by design — a shared machine "can receive incoming connections
  but cannot start connections" — so the operator still cannot reach the guest's machine; flipping that
  needs the guest to share hers back. The share then dies silently at **key expiry** (read it off
  `tailscale status --json`), arriving as "the service broke"; disable key expiry or plan the rotation.
  Say plainly that this step is the operator's: the admin console wants SSO, there is no `tailscale
  share` subcommand, and `funnel` is not the answer (it publishes to the public internet, leaving only
  the password gate). Never add a second `tailscaled` on the host to "make it simpler" — a WSL2 node
  and a host node nest their tunnels and pass no traffic.
- **Timeouts on every client standing in front of a local embedding model**, sized against the
  measured cold start.

## What the second person's client changes

Two clients reach the same runtime; the operator picks, and the choice has architecture consequences.

- **Browser.** The dashboard facade serves the SPA *and* the same JSON-RPC/WS API, so verify this one
  first: `/api/status` reports `auth_required` with the provider list, `/` redirects to `/login`. Nothing
  to install on the other side, and it is the right default for "she should be able to look at it".
- **The desktop app pointed at the runtime** (its "Remote gateway" entry). It discovers a backend
  through the public `/api/status` `auth_required` field and takes its session token off the served
  page; `serve`'s headless mode only skips the SPA mount, so the API it needs is the same on either
  facade. Report that as a code-read conclusion rather than a tested one unless somebody actually
  attached a real app — and if it does not attach, run `serve` on a second loopback port beside the
  dashboard unit (two servers over one `HERMES_HOME` is normal usage) instead of giving up the browser
  UI. **Pitfall:** the app's "Update Hermes" acts on the *connected* backend, so a guest pointed at the
  operator's runtime holds an update button aimed at the operator's machine; it fails on the tenant's
  read-only tree, but tell the guest not to press it.
- **The app with its own local runtime** (the app will install a full runtime into the guest's own
  `HERMES_HOME`; its gateway list holds several backends at once, roster = one row per gateway+profile).
  That configuration **retires the "act on her machine" project**: her own files are handled by her own
  runtime, so no tunnel back to her host, no OpenSSH precondition, no allowlist entry. State the costs in
  the same breath — her own model key or the operator keeps paying, a *Windows* agent with Windows quirks
  instead of the Linux sandbox, a second skill tree (hand over the same denylisted bundle), and **no
  store access**, because the governed gateway stays loopback-only unless the operator deliberately
  exposes it. That last one is a boundary change: flag it, do not perform it.

## Cutting the exposure control over (what to run, in what order)

An exposure control is not deployed until it is exercised through the service that will enforce it,
with the identities that will use it. The order that works:

1. **Mint first, restart second.** Wire the control, `systemctl --user restart <gateway>`, then
   verify — a running gateway executes the module it started with, so an in-process test proves the
   code, not the deployment. The credential file the guest will use must exist and be the flat shape
   above *before* the first live call, or the first call is a misleading 403.
   `systemctl enable --now` is a **no-op on an already-running unit**: an install that writes config
   and then "enables" the service leaves the old process serving the old config, and every check that
   inspects files on disk still passes. Ship `enable` + `restart`, and put a staleness probe in the
   verifier — compare the unit's `ActiveEnterTimestamp` against the mtime of the config it should have
   loaded, and fail when the process is older. "Deployed" and "in effect" are different claims; only
   the second one is worth reporting.
2. **Read the real routes off the server module** instead of guessing them (`/v1/search/{kind}`
   with `query`/`max_items`, `/v1/artifacts/{kind}/{id}`); a wrong path returns `400`, which is easy
   to misread as the control working.
3. **Run the two-identity matrix and keep it as the acceptance record** — owner and guest, both
   paths: the owner's search still returns the withheld records and its by-id fetch still carries the
   reference (the control must not touch the owner's view); the guest's search returns *nothing* for
   a query that plainly matches withheld records, and its by-id fetch of a withheld id returns the
   **same** status as a genuinely non-existent id, or the ids are enumerable.
4. **Write the unit tests in both directions.** Assert that a *clean* reference survives alongside
   the assertion that a withheld one is gone: an over-broad expectation ("provenance is empty")
   passes only against an implementation that destroys provenance wholesale, and when such a test
   fails, check whether the expectation encodes the control's purpose before touching the code.
5. **Put the self-check inside the tooling, not only in the test file.** A mint script asserting
   `identity in json.loads(cred)` costs three lines and converts a silent 403 into a named failure.

## A second tenant on one host: "loopback-only" stops being a boundary

Before calling a borrowed runtime isolated, enumerate every listening socket and issue one
**credential-free** request to each. On a single-tenant host "binds 127.0.0.1" means "only I can reach
it"; with a second tenant on the same machine it means "any local process can" — and the guest's own
tools (web/fetch/browser run *on the host*) are such a process. Services answering 401/403 to a bare
request are fine; the one that answered 200 and **executed** was the operator's own agent endpoint,
whose documented default is "no token ⇒ localhost only" — sound only while there is one tenant.

- Probe with a harmless payload and read the task state, not the HTTP code: `TASK_STATE_COMPLETED`
  plus a real reply proves execution. A model that answers "I cannot verify your identity" is not a
  control, it is a probability (OWASP LLM07: the system prompt is not a security control).
- Fix it with the credential the peer already holds on its own side (per-peer token env + trusted-peer
  allow-list) instead of minting a new secret, so the working link survives; then re-run the probe in
  both arms — bare request must fail, the peer's token must still be accepted — and confirm in the
  audit log that the recorded identity changed from a derived IP to a peer name.
- Closing one socket is a patch, not a premise change. The premise-level fix is per-tenant loopback
  **addresses**: give the guest its own `127.0.0.x`, deny it the rest of `127.0.0.0/8`, and every
  unauthenticated local service retires at once — but its own ingress listener must move too, and a
  tunnel that only proxies to `127.0.0.1` then needs a small local forwarder bridging the two
  addresses. Prefer the credential patch now, the address split when the entry path is designed, and
  always say which one is actually in place.

## Deliverable shape: one idempotent installer, one probe per claim

Ship the whole tenant as **one idempotent script directory** in the operator's tree with modes
`plan | --apply | --verify | --uninstall`, and keep it as the reviewable source of truth rather than
as shell history. Plan mode must work **without** root, and `--apply` must be safe to re-run (it is
the only thing the operator will run after any change). Files, by role:

| File | Role |
|---|---|
| `install.sh` | the four modes; rewrites path prefixes while copying the profile into the runtime home, then asserts no operator-home path survived the copy |
| `sync-<tenant>-skills.py` | copies the operator's skill tree into the runtime home minus a denylist, root-owned read-only, and **deletes** what the denylist or the source no longer contains (a denylist addition that does not take effect is worse than no denylist) |
| `<tenant>-skills-denylist.txt` | one path per line with the *reason* as a comment; the operator edits this file, never the sync script |
| `<tenant>-guard.py` + `shell-hooks-allowlist.json` | the quota/audit gate and its byte-identical pre-seeded approval |
| `<tenant>-gate-watch.sh` + a systemd timer | reconciliation for the declaration files the runtime itself must be able to write |
| `matplotlibrc-<tenant>` | per-tenant plotting defaults (font fallbacks, `pdf.fonttype: 42`) for a runtime that cannot read the operator's `~/.config` |

In this deployment they sit in `~/hermes/setup/guest-structural-layer/` beside `ARCHITECTURE.md`
(long-form design: the boundaries, the status table, the known exposures) and `README.md` (why each
choice). Update both docs in the same pass as the code — the status table is what the operator reads
before re-running, and a stale one is how "deployed but not in effect" gets reported as done.

Probe discipline, which is what makes `--verify` worth running at all:

- Every claim gets a probe that runs **as the tenant identity** (`runuser -u <tenant> -- …`), not as
  root reading a config. A probe that reads the config proves the config, not the boundary.
- Measure boundaries by **enumerating and counting the negative space**
  (`find <operator home> -type f -readable` must be 0 outside the code tree the tenant needs), never
  by spot-checking paths — spot checks miss the hundreds of thousands of files a single ACL or
  `chmod` slip exposes.
- Use a *read* command for read tests: `ls <file>` succeeds on a stat alone and reports "allowed" for
  a file the tenant cannot open. Read bytes (`head -c 1 <file>`).
- End-to-end capability probes beat dependency probes: one probe that renders a figure with a label
  in the tenant's own language covers "package installed" + "interpreter readable" + "fonts
  configured" in one line, and it is the probe that would have caught this deployment's first outage.
- A tamper-restoring watcher needs its own probe too (see the gate section) — a watcher that fires on
  a healthy state restarts the service every few minutes and reads as a flapping service.
- **A refusal you cannot attribute is not evidence.** A probe that must come back *denied* needs its
  scaffolding readable and writable **by the tenant** (scratch dir owned by the tenant, not root), or a
  fail-closed control's refusal is indistinguishable from the probe's own permissions. Run the control's
  happy path as the tenant once, then the denied path: only the second run is about the control.

## In effect, and still up after a reboot

Two acceptance checks that file-based verification never catches:

- **Read the runtime's effective properties, not the unit file you just wrote.**
  `systemctl show <unit> -p MemoryMax -p CPUQuotaPerSecUSec -p TasksMax -p ProtectProc -p ProcSubset`
  prints what the service is actually running with — the same "deployed vs in effect" gap as the
  config-staleness probe, one layer lower. `journalctl -u <unit>` then catches what the new settings
  broke, which for a tenant gaining a shell means permission errors on read-only trees it now writes
  into by accident.
- **On a host that loses power regularly, boot survival is part of "it works".** Check `is-enabled`
  on the tenant's *system* unit and its reconciliation **timer**, on the tunnel daemon, and the
  tunnel's persistent config (`tailscale serve status`) — plus `loginctl show-user <operator> -p
  Linger` for the operator's own *user-level* services, which otherwise stay down after a power cut
  until somebody logs in. Report the recovery chain as one list: the tenant's outage window and the
  operator's scheduled jobs both hang off it.

## Running the privileged part

Hermes has **no password-prompt surface**: the desktop approval dialog governs *whether a command
may run*, not secrets, so "show me a popup and I'll type the password" cannot be satisfied as
asked. Say that plainly, then offer the two safe paths — (a) hand over the exact command block and
let the operator run it (nothing secret leaves their keyboard), or (b) the operator puts
`SUDO_PASSWORD` in `~/.hermes/.env` themselves, stating the real cost: that file is readable by the
agent's own terminal tool, so it is equivalent to delegating sudo, and the plaintext sits on disk.
Never ask for, accept, or repeat a password in chat, whatever the operator offers.

Two properties make such a script worth running: the plan mode must work **without** root ("look
before you change" is for everyone, and a plan that needs root is one nobody reviews), and it must
**adopt an already-minted credential** rather than minting a second one (re-minting invalidates the
token that was just verified end to end).

**Split the work by what needs the operator's hands, and finish everything else before replying.**
He says some version of "do the part on my side that you can do" on every pass of a multi-session
build, so the shape to deliver is: do every step that does not require his console, his identity or
a secret first; hand back the shortest possible remaining list ("two clicks", or one command block),
not the plan; pre-write the artifact he has to forward (a ready-to-send message with placeholders
for the parts only he can fill, and never the secret itself); and resolve by reading code or docs
any question you could answer yourself instead of asking it. One line each on why a remaining step
is his — a missing credential or an admin console — is enough.

## Giving the tenant a shell (and the skills to use it)

A tenant with no execution surface cannot even run `ls`; when it cannot run a script it may
**hand-write the artifact and present it as the tool's output** (observed: six figures requested,
two hand-drawn SVGs delivered, because the plotting stack was missing and the shell was unconnected).
Put the honesty rule in the tenant's SOUL: "say 'this can't run here', never fake an artifact".

- **Prefer a local backend inside the tenant's own OS user** over reaching into the operator's
  machine: `ProtectSystem=strict` + `ReadWritePaths=<tenant home>` + `InaccessiblePaths=<operator
  dirs>` already make it a sandbox, and child processes inherit it. Before granting the shell add
  `ProtectProc=invisible` + `ProcSubset=pid` (otherwise `ps` shows what the operator is running,
  command lines included) and resource ceilings (`MemoryMax`, `CPUQuota`, `TasksMax`).
- **Give the tenant the operator's skills minus an explicit denylist.** A profile made with
  `--no-skills` has ~0 skills, and no installer step seeds the runtime home's `skills/`, so "the
  tenant can do what I can do" silently fails. Ship them root-owned read-only (the tenant must not
  be able to add or delete skills -- a prompt injection into a skill tree is a real vector) and set
  `skills.curator.enabled: false` (the curator wants to write that tree).
- **Per-runtime plotting config must live where that runtime can read it.** The operator's
  `~/.config/matplotlib/matplotlibrc` is invisible to a unit with `InaccessiblePaths=~/.config`, so
  point `MPLCONFIGDIR` at a dir inside the tenant's home and drop the rc file there (dir writable for
  the font cache, rc file root 0444). Without it every Chinese label renders as a box. Never put the
  override in the package's own `mpl-data/matplotlibrc`: matplotlib parses non-key comment lines
there as keys and prints `Missing colon` / `Duplicate key` on **every** import, and an installer that
hardlinks packages into place (uv) shares that inode with its download cache, so the edit is not
even local to the venv.
- **uv installs by hardlink, and hardlinks do not inherit the parent directory's default ACL.**
  Packages installed *after* the ACL grant stay unreadable by the tenant, surfacing later as a
  random ImportError inside the tenant's runtime. Re-run `setfacl -R -m u:<tenant>:rX <venv>` after
  any install, and keep a verify probe that counts unreadable files under the venv.

## The gate must not be owned by the process it gates

"A quota/audit gate is installed" and "the tenant cannot remove it" are two different claims. A
shell-hook gate is a **declaration inside the tenant's own config**, and the tenant's file tools run
in the host process — so it can rewrite `config.yaml`, the hook script, and the allowlist. Two
layers fix this and they are not interchangeable:

- **Ownership (passive):** hook script `root:root 0555`, allowlist `root:root 0644`. Prove the read
  path tolerates it before claiming it works: in Hermes, `agent/shell_hooks.py` `load_allowlist()`
  swallows `OSError` into an empty skeleton and `save_allowlist()` catches `OSError` and only logs,
  so a read-only allowlist cannot break the runtime. Read the loader/writer — don't assume.
- **Periodic reconciliation (active):** files Hermes itself must write (`config.yaml`, `.env`) cannot
  be chmod'd read-only; a config the runtime cannot write breaks on the next migration. Instead run a
  root systemd timer (`OnBootSec` + every 5 min) that checks the declaration is intact — hook command
  string present verbatim, `fail_closed: true`, the disabled toolsets still disabled — and restores
  from the source profile + restarts on drift. Check the *structure* (`platform_toolsets.cli` via
  yaml), never a whole-file grep: the config also carries a `known_builtin_toolsets` list that
  contains those names and produces false "tampered" alarms.
- Wire the watcher into `--verify`: a watcher that reports drift on a healthy state restarts the
  service every 5 minutes and presents as "the service keeps flapping".

## A read-only tenant + "build it if missing" = guaranteed failure

Any launcher that falls back to *building* (or downloading, or first-run-generating) when a prebuilt
artifact is missing will fail for a tenant with read-only access to the code tree. The symptom looks
like a feature being broken ("Chat unavailable"), and the real error is in the service log, not the
UI. Fix by pointing the unit at the already-built artifact — e.g. `HERMES_TUI_DIR=<repo>/ui-tui`, so
`_make_tui_argv` takes the "prebuilt dist" branch — never by widening write access. Generalize:
enumerate every first-run-generates-X path in the tenant's stack and pin it; the operator's own
session never hits these because it can write.

## When plan mode hangs, suspect the heredoc

A bash heredoc with an **unquoted delimiter** expands its body, so a backtick inside a comment
becomes a real command substitution — and inside `$(cat <<EOF … EOF)` it actually executes. It can
start a server and hang the script; `bash -n` stays clean, only running it exposes the bug. Use
`「」` (or quotes) for code words in comment text inside unquoted heredocs, and read "plan mode took
25s and printed `/chat: No such file or directory`" as this bug rather than a slow machine. After
the bad run, check for stray processes (`pgrep -af`) before re-running.

# Identity authentication, and the migration to it

## The failure mode to probe for

An auth layer that maps the presented token *straight to the identity* (`if token in self.actors`)
makes the literal identity name the credential. Every role boundary the design leans on —
human-only approve, author ≠ verifier, trusted producer — is then a request rather than an
enforcement, because anything that can reach the listener can claim any identity.

Probe it in one line before trusting any boundary: present the literal name as the token. A `200`
means names are still credentials, whatever the documentation says.

## Target state

- One random token per identity (`secrets.token_urlsafe(32)`), minted for **all** identities.
- The store keeps only `sha256:<hex>` (`qa/identity_tokens.json`). Hashes are not secrets and may
  travel with the artifacts.
- Plaintext lives **outside the versioned tree**, mode 0600, in the owner's credential area. The
  store is a git work tree that gets published; plaintext must never be committed.
- The gateway compares hashes with `hmac.compare_digest`, not `==`.
- Legacy acceptance (a name used as a token) is an explicit switch, defaulting to accepting during
  the migration and refusing once flipped.

## The migration, in order

1. **Mint for every identity before flipping anything.** A partial table locks out whoever is
   missing the moment names stop working.
2. **Teach the gateway hash-first while names still work.** Restart and prove all four paths before
   touching any other tool: minted token → 200, literal name → 200 (legacy on), unknown string →
   403, valid token without the scope → 403.
3. **Move each credential holder**, one at a time, re-checking after each: the read MCP entry, the
   write MCP entry, every CLI tool whose default actor is a name, and the peer-side tool that files
   artifacts. Each holds its own copy of the string; none of them reads the store's hash table.
4. **Flip the switch off**, restart, and re-run the read-surface acceptance plus the adapter suite.
   A name token must now be refused, and a refusal must be `403` — never `500`.
5. Keep the plaintext file 0600 and out of the repository, and rotate it if it may have leaked.

## Consequences to fix afterwards

- **Re-key trust lists.** A list that reads `created_by` from the artifact body is written by the
  submitter; enforcement has to come from the authenticated identity or from the audit log's record
  of who actually filed the artifact.
- **A `500` on every token is an edit bug, not an auth decision.** A missing stdlib import
  (`hmac`, `hashlib`, `os`) in the auth path turns clean refusals into server errors that look like
  a dead gateway. Fix the import and re-probe all four paths.
- **Expect query-string curl recipes to break at the flip.** Any snippet that passes the identity
  name as `X-Intelligence-Token` is a migration-era shortcut; read the actor's real token from its
  credential file instead of typing the name.
- **Two files share the name `identity_tokens.json`, and only one holds a usable token.** The copy in
  the store holds hashes; the plaintext lives in the credential file outside it. A smoke test that
  reads the store's copy and sends its value as the token gets `403` and makes a correct
  implementation look broken — check *which* file you read before debugging the auth code at all.
- **Settle a refusal arithmetically before suspecting the code.** Compute
  `sha256:<hex>` for the token you hold and compare it with the entry the index holds, in-process:
  equal digests plus a `403` means the transport or the token source is wrong, unequal digests mean
  the token was never the one that was minted. That one comparison replaces a round of guessing, and
  it also distinguishes "the index is empty" (a path or env-var problem) from "the index is right".
- **Report the state, not the intent.** Until the switch is off, say "names are still credentials"
  rather than describing the system as authenticated.
- **The credential file is a flat map `{identity: plaintext}` — a nested writer fails silently.**
  The client resolves with `json.loads(path).get(identity)`; a file written as
  `{"scheme": …, "tokens": {"<identity>": …}}` (or any wrapper) resolves to nothing, and the
  fallback is the identity *name*, so the only visible symptom is the gateway's `403 unknown
  identity token`. A mint script must therefore verify its own output **shape** — read the file back
  and assert `identity in json.loads(...)` — not just the hash round-trip; those are different
  assertions and only the second one catches this. And never fix it by re-minting: re-minting
  rotates the token you just verified, so reshape the existing plaintext in place (copy it aside
  first).
- **A harness that sets one identity's credential path for a whole process de-authenticates every
  other identity in it.** Exporting `INTELLIGENCE_TOKENS` once and resolving two identities from
  that single process makes the second one fall back to its name, so a perfectly working owner
  identity reports `403` and the run looks like a boundary breach that is not there. Resolve each
  identity's token from its own credential file, and print only `len(token)` plus a
  `token != identity_name` boolean — enough to catch the fallback without putting a secret in the
  transcript.

# MCP access surface: one URL every agent can read

The store already answers a bounded HTTP API and a stdio MCP adapter. Neither is a
"read it from anywhere" surface: each runtime wires its own subprocess, token and tool
whitelist, so the third agent costs a third copy. The protocol's 2025-06-18 revision
defines **Streamable HTTP** — one endpoint path, POST carrying JSON-RPC, auth at the
transport layer — which is what makes "any client, one line of config" true.

## Deployed shape

All on `127.0.0.1:8765` (the gateway's own process; no second service to supervise).

| path | method | auth | behaviour |
|---|---|---|---|
| `/mcp` | POST | Bearer | `initialize` / `ping` / `tools/list` / `tools/call` / `resources/list` / `resources/read` / `prompts/list` |
| `/mcp` | GET | — | **405**. No server-initiated stream; the spec allows a basic server to decline it |
| `/.well-known/mcp.json` | GET | none | discovery: transport, url, auth shape, protocol version |
| `/healthz` | GET | none | one bit: the listener is up |

The implementation is `gateway/mcp_http.py` (pure dispatch, testable without a socket)
plus a branch in the experimental API handler. Keep dispatch a table keyed on method
name, not an if/elif ladder — MCP adds methods over time and each one should be a row.

## Tools and resources

| tool | note |
|---|---|
| `search_knowledge` | omit `kind` to search all four kinds; merge results by score |
| `get_artifact` | one record by kind + id, with provenance |
| `kb_index` | approved ids/titles/tags per kind — cheaper than a blind search when the caller does not know what exists |
| `deposit_candidate` | creates a **candidate** only; admission decides. A client must not be able to approve its own deposit |

Resources: `kb://index` and `kb://{kind}/{id}`. Mark read-only tools with
`annotations.readOnlyHint` — clients use it to decide what may run without a prompt,
and `trust: untrusted` then prompts only on the write tool, which is the free human gate.

`resources/list` enumerates the approved corpus, so cap or paginate it once the store
grows past a few hundred records; every record also appearing in `kb_index` is the
intended redundancy, not a bug.

## Auth and transport hardening

- Bearer token resolves to an `Actor`; what is readable follows the identity, never the URL.
  Accept `X-Intelligence-Token` as well so existing scripts keep working.
- **Validate `Origin`** when present, allowing only loopback hosts — the spec requires it
  specifically to stop DNS rebinding against a local server.
- Bind `127.0.0.1` only (already enforced by `build_server`).
- Notifications (`notifications/initialized`, `notifications/cancelled`) return **202 with no
  body**. Returning a JSON-RPC object makes strict clients treat the session as broken.
- Unknown method → `-32601`; unknown resource → `-32002` with the uri in `data`. Tool
  failures are *results* (`isError: true`), not protocol errors — a bad query must not
  tear down the session.

## Client configuration

```jsonc
// Hermes (~/.hermes/config.yaml, mcp_servers)
intelligence:
  url: http://127.0.0.1:8765/mcp
  headers: {Authorization: "Bearer <TOKEN>"}
  trust: untrusted
  tools: {include: [search_knowledge, get_artifact, kb_index]}

// mcporter (any MCP host)
{"mcpServers": {"kb": {"url": "http://127.0.0.1:8765/mcp",
  "headers": {"Authorization": "Bearer <TOKEN>"}}}}
```

`tools/kb_connect.py --check` runs the three probes that matter (endpoint alive, token
resolves, content readable) and `--print-config hermes|openclaw|mcporter` emits the block.
Prefer it to hand-editing config: it prints the token, so say out loud that the output
must not be committed.

**Keep the stdio adapter for runtimes already wired.** It resolves the identity from the
credential file and therefore never puts a plaintext token in a config file. The HTTP
endpoint is for the *next* agent, not a reason to re-plumb working ones.

## Verification: use a client you did not write

Own probe passing proves the envelope, not interoperability. Check all three:

1. **This agent's built-in MCP** — call the read tool from the running session; the result
   naming a record you filed minutes ago is the end-to-end proof.
2. **A third-party implementation** — `mcporter` (Node): `list <name> --schema`, `call
   <name>.search_knowledge query=...`, `resource <name> kb://index`. Three different code
   paths through the same server.
3. **The other local runtime** — `openclaw mcp probe` reports the tool count.

Then the negative cases in one pass: no token → 403, foreign `Origin` → 403, `GET /mcp` →
405, `/.well-known/mcp.json` without a token → 200. A surface that answers only the happy
path has not been tested.

# Hybrid Retrieval: design, measurement, and the constants that bite

Where it lives: `AI_Platform/intelligence/gateway/retrieval.py` (BM25 + embeddings +
weighted RRF + relevance gate + optional reranker), constructed by
`gateway/service.py::_build_retriever`. Stdlib only - no numpy, no vector store:
at this corpus size brute-force cosine over cached vectors beats a round trip to a
vector database, and the gateway runs under the system python.

## Two invariants that outrank quality

1. **Filter, then rank.** Permission/status/scope filtering happens in the service
   (`_search_documents`) before the retriever sees anything. The retriever is handed
   exactly what the caller may read, so no score, trace or count can leak the
   existence of a candidate to a reader without candidate scope. Never move a filter
   into the ranking layer.
2. **Degrade, never fail.** If the embedder is unreachable the search still returns
   BM25 results with `mode: lexical` and a note. A knowledge base that stops
   answering because a model server restarted is worse than one that answers with
   lexical matches and says so.

## Procedure: measure before touching a constant

1. Run the harness: `python3 /mnt/d/OpenClaw/tools/intelligence-retrieval-eval.py
   --corpus synthetic --modes lexical,vector,hybrid` (add `hybrid+rerank` to price a
   reranker). It builds a labelled synthetic corpus - themes, distractor documents
   that share vocabulary with the right answer, identifiers, version strings, error
   codes, Chinese and English paraphrases of the same thing - plus negative queries
   that must return nothing.
2. Read `recall@1`, `recall@5`, `MRR` **and** `neg-leak` together. neg-leak is the
   share of unrelated queries that still return hits. Optimising recall alone is how
   you get a retriever that always answers, confidently and uselessly.
3. Sweep the knob through the environment, cheapest first:
   `INTELLIGENCE_EMBED_MODEL`, `INTELLIGENCE_RRF_K`, `INTELLIGENCE_RRF_WEIGHTS`,
   `INTELLIGENCE_MIN_COSINE`, `INTELLIGENCE_MIN_IDF_RATIO`.
4. Tune where differences are still visible. A benchmark that returns 1.000 for
   every configuration has stopped measuring anything - add a harder tier or more
   negative queries instead of tuning on a saturated set, then re-check that the
   chosen values do not cost anything on the strong configuration.
5. `--corpus live` is a smoke check, not a metric: the labelled queries belong to
   the synthetic corpus, so recall against the real store is meaningless. Use it to
   confirm short and identifier queries still resolve and that unrelated ones do not.
   **A benchmark is a measurement, not a reader.** In `live` mode it fetches through the
   normal read path, so it emits `used` events and bumps surfacing counters exactly like a
   person; one such run kept the "nobody is reading this" alarm silent for a week. Set the
   telemetry-suppression switch in the harness itself (this install:
   `INTELLIGENCE_TELEMETRY_SUPPRESS=1`), and verify it by recording the event-file line
   count around a run.

Two traps that decide whether a result means anything. When a change makes no
difference, **inspect the fixture before the hypothesis**: a "long broad document"
fixture originally built from the same sentences as the specific documents wins
legitimately and measures nothing about the change under test - and getting no
difference is a result to report, not a reason to ship the intuition. When a hit
exposes a better reading of a query than the label did, **accept both answers and
record why** instead of editing the expectation into passing; the label was the
finding.

**Where the live values come from: read the construction site, never the signature.**
`Retriever.__init__` in `retrieval.py` carries *library* defaults (`rrf_k=60`,
`min_cosine=0.55`) that are **not** in force here. The values that run are set where the
retriever is built, `gateway/service.py::_build_retriever`, each one an env override with a
measured default: `INTELLIGENCE_EMBED_MODEL=bge-m3`, `INTELLIGENCE_RRF_K=10`,
`INTELLIGENCE_RRF_WEIGHTS=1.0,0.25`, `INTELLIGENCE_MIN_COSINE=0.50`,
`INTELLIGENCE_MIN_IDF_RATIO=0.6`, `INTELLIGENCE_CHUNK=1`,
`INTELLIGENCE_PASSAGE_CHARS=600`, `INTELLIGENCE_RERANK=none`.
**The `systemd` unit is not where they live on this install** - `systemctl --user show -p
Environment` carries only the state dir and the legacy-names switch, so an absent variable
there proves nothing about the value in force. This is the same shape as the auto-admission
mode, whose authority is a file in the store rather than the process environment: when a
setting can be declared in three places (signature default, construction-site default, unit
environment), grep the construction site before quoting any number or debugging any
behaviour.

## Constants that assume a scale (each of these was wrong when copied)

- **RRF `k`.** The paper's `k=60` pools rankings thousands of documents deep. On a
  corpus of dozens, every candidate lands inside the top 20 of both retrievers, the
  `1/(k+rank)` terms flatten out, and fusion degenerates into counting votes - it
  scored *worse* than lexical alone. Use ~10 here and re-measure when the corpus
  grows an order of magnitude.
- **Fusion weights.** Rank-based fusion treats both retrievers as equally
  trustworthy. When one is measurably weaker on this corpus, declare it:
  `INTELLIGENCE_RRF_WEIGHTS=1.0,0.25` (lexical carries precision, the vector half
  carries recall).
- **A lexical gate on raw BM25 score or absolute idf.** idf is unbounded and shrinks
  as a corpus grows, so a floor calibrated on one corpus size silently kills short
  queries (`403`, `v2.0.1`, `pit`) on another. Gate on *relative* distinctiveness:
  matched idf >= ratio x the best idf available for that query in this corpus.
- **A vector gate on cosine is safe to make absolute** because cosine is bounded, so
  a threshold transfers across corpus sizes. Measured separation on this corpus:
  relevant pairs 0.40-0.79, unrelated 0.13-0.60, overlapping - so the floor is the
  recall-vs-leak dial (0.45 -> recall 1.000 / leak 0.375; 0.50 -> 0.917 / 0.000;
  0.55 -> 0.833 / 0.000). Default 0.50. State the trade-off next to the constant;
  picking a point on that curve is a policy choice, not a technical one.
- **A gate is not optional.** "Rank everything and return the top k" makes every
  query look answered: dense vectors are positively similar to almost anything. That
  hands an agent confident-looking irrelevant context *and* buries the zero-result
  signal, which is the most actionable thing this knowledge base emits.

## Chunking (passages)

`split_passages` cuts `title + content` into passages of ~600 chars (hard cap 1400):
whole sentences are packed up to the target and only a sentence that cannot fit the
cap is fragmented; short paragraphs merge. Every passage gets its own vector, an
artifact scores on its **best** passage, and the trace names it
(`why.passage: "3/5"`).

- **The split must be deterministic.** Cached vectors are mapped back to passages by
  *index*, so a splitter that varies between calls attributes a vector to the wrong
  passage. Nothing ambient (model, clock, query) may enter the split.
- **The cache carries a format tag (`passages-v1`).** A cache written in the older
  one-vector-per-document shape is dropped rather than reinterpreted as a
  single-passage document; bump the tag whenever the splitting changes.
- **A document's passages are embedded in one request and cached together**, so a
  partial set can never break the index-to-passage mapping.
- The vector half now sees the tail of a long artifact at all. The lexical half
  already could - which is why it scored 1.00 on the past-the-window fixture in both
  configurations, and why chunking read as "no gain" to anyone looking only at that
  number: it removes an asymmetry, it does not add a capability BM25 lacked.

## Embedding model choice is a language question

`nomic-embed-text` is English-first: alone it scored recall@1 0.312 on a
Chinese-language corpus where `bge-m3` scored 0.958, same queries, same pipeline.
Pick the embedder for the corpus language and verify it with the harness rather
than by reputation; a local model was sufficient here, so no external API was
needed. Watch the task-prefix contract - `search_document:` / `search_query:` are
part of nomic's documented usage, while bge-m3 takes none - and derive the prefix
from the model family instead of hardcoding it at a call site.

Vectors are cached in `qa/embeddings.json`, keyed by the artifact digest
(`attestation.artifact_digest`), so an edit re-embeds automatically and an
unchanged artifact never pays twice; changing the model discards the whole cache,
because mixing two models' vectors in one similarity computation produces
silence-free nonsense. Embed at most a bounded number of new documents per search so
a bulk import cannot stall the read path.

## Reranking

Implemented and off by default: `INTELLIGENCE_RERANK=ollama` scores candidates with
a local model, `=http` posts to a Jina/Cohere-style `/rerank`. Keep it off until the
harness discriminates - a reranker costs a generation per candidate and has to beat
the fused order on a set where the fused order is not already perfect.

**An identical score across two modes is a switch that never engaged, not a finding.** A
`hybrid+rerank` run reproduced `hybrid` to three decimals, because the unit sets
`INTELLIGENCE_RERANK=none` and the requested mode never reached the retriever. Before
reporting "reranking adds nothing here", assert which configuration actually ran - print the
mode from the harness output or the retriever's own trace, and check the construction-site
default as above. The same reading applies in reverse: "no gain" from a feature nobody turned
on is the most expensive sentence in a tuning report, because it closes the question.

## Known gaps

- **Chunking fixed the context window, not the broad-document problem - measured, do
  not re-litigate.** Passage-level scoring (now shipped) closes the blind spot where
  an artifact larger than the embedder's window was embedded as its opening only,
  leaving BM25 the sole path to its tail: an answer planted past the truncation point
  went from unfindable to found (0.00 -> 1.00 on that query class), recall@1 rose
  0.839 -> 0.871, MRR 0.887 -> 0.903, at a cost of neg-leak 0.000 -> 0.125. What it
  did **not** do is stop a long, broad document from winning specific queries: once
  the fixture was made genuinely generic (naming themes without containing the
  answers), chunked and unchunked scored identically, and on the live store the broad
  document's winning *passage* is a real passage about the topic - the question is
  answered, not lost. It is a corpus-shape problem. The untested options are the
  cross-encoder reranker and specificity weighting; neither has a measurement behind
  it, so neither is enabled.
- Search surfacing and retrieval are counted separately in `qa/usage.json`; a record
  that is only ever found, never read, shows up in the review flags and should be
  diagnosed as a findability question rather than a content one.
- **A multilingual embedder does not make the corpus cross-lingual.** Measured on the same
  labelled set: `cross-lingual` recall@1 stayed 0.00 for both lexical and hybrid, and
  English paraphrases went 0.00 -> 0.67 only once the vector half was on. A corpus written in
  one language answers asks in that language; treat an English question against a Chinese
  store as a miss to be routed around (ask in the corpus's language), not as a retriever
  defect to tune away.

## Tests

Unit tests run lexical-only: every test module that constructs a gateway sets
`os.environ.setdefault("INTELLIGENCE_EMBED_DISABLE", "1")` before it does. Tests must
not depend on whether a model server happens to be running on the machine, and
`test_retrieval.py` covers the mechanical half (tokenisation, BM25, fusion weights,
cache invalidation on digest and on model swap, degradation, the embed budget) plus
the security half (a candidate must not be counted, ranked or hinted at for a reader
without candidate scope).

# Auditing a running governed store

Order matters: **liveness first**, then supply, then duplication, then hygiene. A report that opens
with code debt buries the only finding that changes behaviour - a store can be technically healthy
and completely unused, and that is the finding the operator needs first.

Every number below must come from a command run in the session that reports it. Docs describe
intent; the store and the unit describe state.

## 0. Fix the state directory before reading anything

The runtime state (audit, events, usage counters, token hashes, embeddings) lives in
`$INTELLIGENCE_STATE`, not in `<root>/qa`. `<root>/qa` keeps a snapshot from whenever the split
happened - plausibly complete-looking and stale - so a report run without the variable prints a
real table built from the wrong days. Set the same value the service unit sets, and check it before
believing any count. `governance-config.json` is the exception: it is read from the store itself.

Symptom to recognise: a usage report whose "last read" dates all cluster on one old day, and a
`reads` column that is uniformly zero. That is a stale-state read, not an idle corpus.

## 1. Liveness: is anything actually being read?

- `events.jsonl`, `action == "used"`, grouped by day: the strong signal (whole record fetched).
- `audit.jsonl` action counts by day: `search_*` / `get_*` are reads, `submit_candidate` /
  `validate_candidate` / `approve` are intake.
- Compare intake against consumption. Writes continuing while reads sit at zero is a corpus that is
  fed and never consulted - a workflow gap, and no threshold change fixes it.
- Before calling a spike "usage", read what produced it: fifty searches inside thirty seconds is a
  benchmark, not a reader. Measurement traffic lands in the same files as real readers, so an
  evaluator pointed at the live store must be able to switch telemetry off — a flag checked at
  write time (`INTELLIGENCE_TELEMETRY_SUPPRESS` here) that gates the event and usage writes and
  never the audit chain. Without it one eval run inflates `reads` and, worse, clears the
  "nobody is reading this" threshold for days.
- Any alarm about consumption must count the action that *is* consumption. Counting `search_*` calls
  lets an evaluator, a duplicate screen or a plain miss clear the threshold; count `used` events,
  and compare timestamps as UTC-aware values — mixing a naive local `now()` with `Z`-stamped records
  shifts the window and hides a stall.

Calibration from a ~45-record store: 70% of all `used` events fell in the build week, the top record
held ~35% of the rest, and 18 days passed with zero - which the weekly report never mentioned.

## 2. Supply: what the corpus is made of

Count per kind and status, then per scope. Release counts, not file counts: a scanned `*.json` tree
includes archived records that no read surface serves.

Then name the **pipe** that fills each kind, and the class of knowledge that pipe cannot carry -
counting records answers "how much", not "why this and not that". A kind fed only by distillation of
another agent's experience contains only what that agent happened to do; a kind whose only gate
demands a declared contract plus a runnable test contains no method-shaped knowledge at all, however
valuable. Measured: every released record sat in one domain while the owner's current main line had
none, and the corpus was healthy by every count - the defect was a missing route, not missing
content. For each empty or thin kind, ask what would have had to happen for a record to appear, and
whether that thing is even possible on this side.

Read the harvester's cursor/watermark file in the same pass: its timestamp is where the next scan
starts, so a cursor pushed forward (by a test run, a clock change, a manual probe) makes the job
skip the real backlog, and its id list is the cheapest place to spot fixture pollution - test ids
like `layout-demo` sitting beside a real one. Check it after any suite run against live state.

Then the flags: `never-used` + `auto-admitted-unverified` together is the zombie signature - policy
admitted it, nobody ever read it. Measure the share of released records carrying it; above ~a third
is an admission-policy problem, not a content problem.

## 3. Duplication: cross-kind, or you will miss it

A screen that iterates one kind at a time cannot see the duplicate that accumulates fastest -
`experience` (raw note) next to the `knowledge` distilled from it, both approved. Scan the union of
kinds in one pass.

Pair by provenance, not similarity: the finished record already cites its source
(`source[].ref = "experience:<id>"`), which is exact, explainable, and free of the false positives
that make a rank-based report ignorable. Use the ranker only to *find candidates*; use the citation
to *prove* the pair.

When a pair has no citation - two records written independently - the verdict is cosine, not rank
agreement: measured on this corpus the real pairs sat at 0.83–0.92 while the nearest unrelated
neighbour never cleared 0.70, whereas the rank window fired on unrelated notes because at a few
dozen documents every probe has something at rank 1. Put the threshold inside that measured gap,
and use the same number for the admission-time duplicate screen so "duplicate" means one thing to
the auditor and to the gate.

## 4. Hygiene

- `git status --porcelain` for `??` under `approved/`: auto-admission writes files and nothing
  commits them, so the canonical tree silently falls behind the store. Count them before claiming
  the repository is the authority.
- Count commit subjects. A daily automated anchor commit per day of history means the log is mostly
  noise and a real change is hard to find; that is a reporting cost, not a bug, but say which it is.
- Compare the unit's `Environment=` with the docs: a migration switch, a state path, a test count,
  or a "still open" limitation is usually stale in prose and current in the unit.
- Verify the verifiers. Run the read-surface acceptance live; if it reports a fistful of failures,
  check the credential before the surface - a checker that defaults to the identity *name* after a
  token migration produces seven failures about a healthy gateway. Expect the self-test and the live
  run to be separately green.
- The fix for Git drift belongs in the maintenance job that already runs daily, not in a new one:
  commit the store paths and the audit anchor together when anything is pending, and fall back to a
  weekly anchor-only commit when nothing is. Filter the owner's excluded paths explicitly in that
  script rather than a broad `git add -A` — a bulk add stages the very records you were told to
  leave out.
- A liveness route that sits behind the same credential as the data routes is not a liveness route:
  no watchdog holds an identity token. Keep the authenticated `/health` and add an unauthenticated
  one-bit `/healthz` that says nothing about the corpus.
- Re-check every finding against the tree before it enters the report. Two plausible claims in one
  review were both wrong: "test leftovers are sitting in `approved/`" (they were in `candidates/`,
  which is the correct layout for every non-approved status) and "the scheduled agent runs on empty
  input and burns model calls" (cron's monitor gate suppresses the agent when the monitored output
  hash is unchanged — `changed=False`, no run — so the job cost a shell script). A wrong finding
  costs more than a missing one, because the fix built on it is wasted work.

## 5. Small API facts that cost time

- `IntelligenceGateway(...)` takes a `Path`; a `str` raises `TypeError` at construction.
- `search()` returns a list; `usage_summary()["explicit"]` is derived from `events.jsonl`, while
  `usage.json` holds only `surfaced` and `misses`. That is why "reads" never appear in the usage
  file and why a report can look internally consistent while reading the wrong state.
- Per-kind getters are `get_knowledge` / `get_experience` / `get_skill` / `get_source`.

## 6. Demand, not only mechanism

A stalled read path has two candidate causes and they look identical in the counters: nothing
*triggers* a lookup, or there is nothing to look up. Before prescribing triggers, compare the
corpus's topics with what the user is working on now. A store full of last quarter's engineering
notes, next to a user whose current work is in another domain entirely, stays unread no matter how
many skill preambles open with "search the KB first". Say it plainly and make it a decision: feed
the current main line, or accept the store as a reference shelf for one class of task.

## 7. Shape of the report

1. One-sentence verdict (alive / used / decaying / stalled).
2. Liveness with the date of the last real read.
3. Supply and the zombie share.
4. Duplication with the exact pairs.
5. Defects, each with the line that manifests it, then a phased fix list.
6. What you changed, and how each change was verified - a fix without a probe is a claim.

# Moving the governed store to another path

The store is referenced from more places than it looks, and the copy is exactly the kind of thing a
botched move leaves doubled. Move, repoint, verify, then freeze the original — in that order, and
never freeze before the new location is serving.

## 1. Find every reference first

Search code and config, not just prose, and search for a **fragment** of the path: a path split
across two adjacent string literals (a wrapped long line) does not match a single-line pattern, so a
whole-path search returns nothing while the dependency is right there.

```bash
rg -l --no-messages -g '!node_modules' -g '!*/source/*' '<path-fragment>' \
  <tool dir> <workspace dir> ~/.config/systemd ~/.hermes /mnt/c/Users/<user>/.codex
```

Expect: the systemd unit (`WorkingDirectory`, `ExecStart --root`, the `Documentation=` URL), every
tool that imports the package or posts to the gateway, prose docs, and **other applications' state
files** (an editor or agent CLI keeps a recent-projects list). Leave third-party state files alone —
report the stale entry instead of editing another tool's state.

The tools that matter here are beside the OpenClaw tree (`tools/intelligence-mcp/`,
`hermes-skill-backflow.py`, `intelligence-approve.py`, `intelligence-validate.py`,
`intelligence-repair-skill-layout.py`).

## 2. Back up, copy, prove the copy byte-for-byte

```bash
tar czf ~/store-backup-pre-move-$(date +%Y%m%d-%H%M%S).tar.gz -C <parent> <dir>
rsync -a --exclude '__pycache__' <src> <dest>/
( cd <src>  && find . -type f -not -path '*__pycache__*' | sort | xargs -d '\n' sha256sum > /tmp/c.sums )
( cd <dest> && find . -type f -not -path '*__pycache__*' | sort | xargs -d '\n' sha256sum > /tmp/d.sums )
diff /tmp/c.sums /tmp/d.sums
```

Exclude the one file a running service appends to (an audit log) from the comparison and say so —
otherwise its growth reads as a mismatch and hides a real one.

Keep whatever parent level the code depends on. If the package is imported as
`from <Platform>.intelligence...`, the copied tree must keep that level, and the suite must be run
with that parent on `sys.path` (`PYTHONPATH=<parent> python3 <Platform>/intelligence/tests/test_x.py`),
or every test breaks at import.

## 3. Repoint — configuration, not surgery

Turn hardcoded roots into env-overridable constants defaulting to the new path
(`INTELLIGENCE_ROOT`, `INTELLIGENCE_PLATFORM`, `INTELLIGENCE_GATEWAY`, plus a token var per
identity). The next move is then a config change. A tool that still hardcodes the root is a defect
to fix while you are in there, not a fact to work around.

Then, for a systemd user unit: edit, `systemctl --user daemon-reload`, restart, and prove where it
actually runs from instead of trusting the restart:

```bash
systemctl --user show -p MainPID --value <unit>
ls -l /proc/<pid>/cwd                              # must be the new root
curl -s -H 'X-Intelligence-Token: <read identity>' http://127.0.0.1:8765/health
```

Finish by running the store's own test suite from the new parent **and** the live acceptance check,
so "it serves" means "it serves correctly". A read-only surface check that passes is the cheapest
proof the move did not change visibility or bounds.

## 4. Freeze the original — and verify it from the Windows side

Rename the old directory (`<dir>.migrated-to-<dest>-<date>`) so a stale duplicate cannot be mistaken
for the live store, then delete it after a few days of clean running.

**On a drvfs mount (`/mnt/c`, `/mnt/d`), a freshly renamed directory can appear in WSL as
`d?????????` with `stat` reporting "No such file or directory", while the data is completely intact.**
That is an unrefreshed directory-entry cache, not data loss. Confirm from the Windows side — before
concluding anything, and especially before telling anyone a directory was destroyed:

```bash
/mnt/c/Windows/System32/cmd.exe /c dir /b "C:\path\to\parent"
/mnt/c/Windows/System32/cmd.exe /c dir /b /s "C:\path\to\renamed\dir"
```

A `dir` that lists the directory means the move succeeded; a WSL `ls` that cannot stat it is the
cache, and a WSL restart clears it. Quoting a path into `cmd.exe /c if exist "..."` is unreliable
from WSL — it answers "missing" for a directory that is there. Use `dir`, which fails loudly.

## Why the backup is not optional

A rename on drvfs can look like a deletion from inside WSL for as long as the cache is stale. The
tar backup taken before the copy is what makes that ambiguity survivable: with it, the worst case is
re-copying; without it, the only evidence is a directory entry you cannot stat.

## Store layout rules

- Non-skill kinds map to `<kind>/approved/<id>.json` when approved, and to `<kind>/candidates/`
  for **every** other status including validated and archived. Because several statuses share one
  directory, a lookup must confirm the file's own `status` before returning it — the path alone
  cannot identify a record's status.
- `kind: skill` maps to `skills/<status>/<id>/manifest.json`; skill directories also hold the body
  and tests beside the manifest.
- Writes are temp-file + atomic replace. No locks, no fsync discipline assumed.

## Status machine

`candidate → experimental → validated → approved → deprecated → archived`.
No candidate→approved shortcut. `approved` requires `verified: true` with `verified_by` and
`verified_at` populated — which only the human approval path sets.

A transition relocates the **whole artifact directory** - manifest, `SKILL.md`, tests and support
files - and rewrites recorded `tests[].path` entries whose prefix was the old status directory. A
transition that moves only the manifest leaves a directory holding files with no `manifest.json`
and a recorded path naming a location that no longer exists; `intelligence-repair-skill-layout.py`
repairs that shape (plan, then `--apply`, iterating to a fixed point) and should otherwise report
nothing to fix.

`verified` may only be true at `approved`, and `approved` requires it: a candidate cannot arrive
pre-verified, and `submit_candidate` refuses an id that already exists in a live status (`approved`
/ `stale` / `deprecated`), auditing the refusal as `id_already_published`. `archived` is excluded on
purpose — the record is inert — so a withdrawn id can be refiled. Updating a published artifact is
therefore a `supersede` (human-held `rollback` scope) or a new id, never a re-submit over the same
id. Withdrawing is the separate move for unpublished artifacts: the status becomes `archived`, the
reason lands in `metadata.withdraw`, the artifact leaves search results, and the check for who may
retract it reads the audit log's last successful submitter rather than `created_by`.
